en: (AIFP Transcript 1061) || {A Compendium of the Essential Meaning of the Four Vedas} ||
To him to whom obeisance is due, whose qualities are complete, whose worship is described in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad,
and who impels our intellect when it is free from enemies— [to him I bow].
Therefore, O Lord, I, having no other refuge, take shelter in you. || 1 ||
Having investigated all the statements that establish [the truth] within the Vedas, their auxiliary branches, or the Tantras,
I compose this compendium of their essential meaning.
Be gracious to me; lead me by the straight path.
This very mass of words— which is divided manifoldly into mantras, arthavādas, and injunctions, and which is an authoritative means of knowledge by virtue of its independence—
has had the reality of its supreme purpose discerned by those free from envy.
The Veda reveals you alone as the Lord. || 3 ||
O Lord, this word "Īśvara," which has come within the range of the Vedas,
makes you alone understood— none other than you who possess a blue throat and are adorned with a crescent moon— for it nourishes its own inherent meaning.
Furthermore, another [type of meaning] is obtained by means of constraining [the literal sense] through context and so forth. (4)
This word is your designation; lexicographers call it a synonym for "Śiva" and so forth, as they do with other terms,
yet it is the very nature of the reality itself that constitutes its state of being worshipful.
Maheśvara says: "The Word is great, supreme, and transcendent. || 5 ||
That which has this as its subordinate element— whether it be the supreme or the great—
is capable of denoting that object in an excellent manner;
being associated with the word "pūjya" (venerable), it is [so] designated by the term.
If those who know the word [the grammarians] are an authority, they declare that it is *pūjā* (worship). || 6 ||

This universe cannot possibly be without a Lord, nor can it have an external Lord, for that would be utterly contrary to the authoritative means of knowledge; since such an external Lord is excluded by both worldly experience and the Veda.
What is this delusion? Some say that the Lord is something else. (7)
The Sāṃkhya declares this entire world to be without a Lord, while Yoga asserts it to be with a Lord; others are merely repeaters of these two views.
However, those who claim the existence of a Lord [as an independent creator] cannot possibly be consistent.
By means of the lotus posture and others, which are designated by the term "non-supreme" (anīśvara). || 8 ||
That sovereignty of yours— foremost, imperishable, free from bondage, and delightful to all beings— which you alone possess as its vessel,
is for the most part a statement indeed difficult to find even in the Vedas.
Except where there is an occasion for your name "Namo" [to be uttered]. || 9 ||
O Lord, the salutations of men have you as their sole object, for we determine that they are directed toward you alone by the power of scripture;
even though those same salutations are prescribed for other deities, they do not belong to them.
Like rivers into the ocean, all streams flow into you.

To whom the Vedic revelation, having proclaimed "Obeisance," spoke of you as the one who binds the sacrificial animal— O Kapardin— and another [revelation] likewise addressed you, O divine young porpoise.
In this way, it is possible to offer salutation by means of both. || 11 ||

Even those of dull intellect, as they perceive you alone— the one who bears the weight of the world— being proclaimed by both their ears from every direction, what [calamity] could possibly befall them?
Even at midday, they might deny the existence of the sun.
O wielder of the trident, it is karma alone that brings you— the Bull of the Trident—
to all your mantras;
for they are characterized by the act of saluting you.
For whom shall we immolate the sacrificial animal? Who is there that has not been made to sacrifice? || 13 ||
O Lord, since you alone remain as the head of the *śiṃśumāra* while all other limbs have been refined by other deities,
it is fitting that homage should now be paid to you.
Not at all for another god, nor for one who is not the Lord. || 14 ||
The *vajriṇī*, the *śaṅkaraśaṅkhinī*, the *mudrā*, and the *kamalinī* taught by Bharata— through these,
there come to be the dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) for those within the assembly of the wise.
With their heads touching [the ground] and their hands joined in the *añjali* mudrā, they [worship] him. || 15 ||
We have heard that some name has been bestowed upon you by the deities as the ultimate ground for all salutations; yet,
O Desired One, there is nothing else capable of receiving those salutations.
To wear the crown as if it were brought by a thief. || 16 ||
"Salutation be to him where you sit"— by this verse, O Maheśa, everything worthy of salutation is addressed; thus,
we offer our salutations toward the primordial medicine.
By which you abide within everything, like an embodied being abiding within a body. || 17 ||
Considering that the entire world is presided over by you alone,
those [demons] fell upon the ears of dogs and their masters;
yet in this world, through the power of your yoga of devotion to Maheśvara—
Even though we have been elevated [to this position], we remain worthy of great respect. || 18 ||
To one who reflects upon it, two kinds of homage appear in the world and in the Vedas, which possess different forms:
that which is directed toward you is prompted by your lordship.
If that [result] produced by contact with them occurs even among those who lack a Lord (īśvara). || 19 ||
The use of the honorific "namas" is generally observed toward both superiors and inferiors solely because of their proximity to oneself;
it is impossible to conceive that it is employed on account of their preeminence.
Thus have the salutations to those who are not the most excellent been demonstrated. || 20 ||
Indeed, even though your name is joined with "supremacy," you are the supreme one because you are the Lord of the fire-eaters (the gods) and of the inviolable ones;
O Blessed One, you are renowned for your supremacy without distinction.
And among the Sāma-gānas, when the mantras are recited with difficulty. || 21 ||

Even for one who desires a son, the offering of *caru* made together with the moon-crested Lord [Śiva] is not sufficient for your satisfaction when performed along with other gods who are merely paying homage; rather, it leads only to the opposite result.
We have heard from Soma that Rudra is Agni. || 22 ||
Indeed, having introduced Agni, he employs the word "Rudra"; that constitutes the Brāhmaṇa portion, for there is a joint invocation of the two.
Here, their separate invocation is clearly observed.
Those who know the hymns recite: "That which [is offered] in the morning to Agni... (RV 10.91.1).

Lest there arise a suspicion that Maheśvara’s power might be coextensive with fire and the other elements, the mantra— which is naturally capable of being construed— must be connected even with the primordial matter (prakṛti), by setting aside the verb and joining it with another word.
May they invoke you for the sake of penance; it does not break the established order.
Because he was cast down from his dwelling by the immortals through the power of the Vasus,
and having arrived at the earth, he wept— therefore he is Rudra, the fire;
or because the Maruts are his own offspring, they are his hosts (gaṇas).
I do not consider you to be anything other than Rudra, the one who is more compassionate than Rudra.
Even in the sacrifice, the word *rudra* is mentioned in the *Āruṇaketuka* [section];
they remember that word as referring to the Lord (*īśvara*), as belonging to Him, and even as His own—
occupying the place of the word *rudra* in that context.
We have heard the sound of the sacrifice from the Sāma-singers. || 26 ||
They say that the term *viṣamekṣaṇa* (the odd-eyed one) and *rudra* (the weeper) are applied to the "uneven" (*viṣama*) fever because it intensely heats and causes one to weep;
furthermore, it is either of a fierce (*raudra*) nature or is a representation thereof.
It becomes another word, similar to the word "vāyasa" (crow). || 27 ||
There indeed exist many formations derived from the suffix -taddhita or the suffix -yat that resemble the word *bhāvata* and are similar to *sāttvata*;
the form of the word "Bhagavān" might well be just like that.
Even the wealth arising from the performance of the sixfold policy does not go to anyone other than you. || 28 ||
Sovereignty that is free from decline, prosperity, wisdom, heroism, fame, and dispassion— these qualities,
O Lord of Qualities, are designated by the term "Bhaga."
We do not wander, O Blessed One; you are indeed the Blessed One. || 29 ||

The term "Īśvara" denotes your sovereignty; the word "Rudra" signifies your valor; and the term "Śiva" expresses your fame. Furthermore, the words "Sarvajña" (All-Knowing) and "Kāmaripu" (Foe of Desire) are employed to denote you.
O Destroyer of the Cities, both omniscience and freedom from passion exist in you.
O Śiva, no one is disenchanted with you who perform purposeful action;
thus you are the most excellent. You are like the *Daśatayī* (the ten-fold Veda), which is empty [of worldly objects] yet moves toward the sage to obtain wealth in its wondrous form.
They declare that it was worshipped by you along with the Maruts.
Truth, forbearance, fortitude, steadfastness, self-knowledge, creative power, dispassion, austerity, intelligence, and lordship—
these never depart from you, nor does dharma ever leave you.
What is there that does not happen for you among those esteemed for their virtues? || 32 ||
O Maheśvara, [this] glory does not come from the naive, nor from the great, nor from heroes,
nor even from illustrious sovereigns who rule the entire earth; it comes from those who are unlike others— those who are free from passion.
The Buddhas proclaim this of the Blessed One, who possesses wisdom. || 33 ||
The Atharvaṇas, proclaiming the teaching that subdues passion,
declare your names as "Bhagavān.
The Upaniṣad of the Atimāśrama calls you Bhageśvara.
And the Nairmaṇḍukas desire to worship the Blessed One. || 34 ||
O Maheśa, worship has been prescribed for you by those who praise you with devotion, performed through mantra and bound to speech, mind, and body;
it is also taught as a form of meditation (upāsanā) by all the Upaniṣads.
Let us contemplate the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad. || 35 ||
Whether the statement you uttered refers to meditation upon that which is within the small space, or whether it cooks for him an equal distinction of form—
even by means of the internal meanings suitable for that purpose— [it is so].
"It must be concealed by words"—this is the proverb of those who know the rules of speech. || 36 ||
I do not find in any way here either the statement that Nārāyaṇa is to be worshipped, or his fruit;
for that which is enjoined by the originative injunction (utpatti-śiṣṭa) cannot go elsewhere.
O Maheśvara, it is not possible for me to perform worship unto you.
This is not an act of worship, nor is the subject of worship even remotely present; therefore, by the method of elimination, it is established that he is the worshipper.
This is because of the statement regarding the Supreme Self as being "situated within."
Even in the absence of the word [denoting it], that state of being its worshiper is established.
Even though the Supreme Self resides within his heart, that which is the Self is not designated as the "Supreme Self" for him; for it is by itself,
within its own mind, like the flame within a fire, [that it is perceived].
"Let him remain as one to be venerated"—at such a word of his, who would not laugh? 39.
That which was described as the heart in the section concerning Nārāyaṇa must belong to him alone and not to another;
for it is observed that in the section concerning ascetics, it is accepted by ascetics.
That meditation which was prescribed for you in the preceding section. || 40 ||
He is called Brahmā, the Supreme, the Ultimate Reality, the Supreme Light, and the Supreme Lord Padmanābha;
he whose sole delight is in meditating upon You, whose state is non-dual with You.
Just as a mantra-practitioner becomes Garuḍa through the meditation on Garuḍa. || 41 ||
In the Gītās, for the purpose of manifesting the power born of yoga, Nārāyaṇa spoke these words aloud to Śivana:
"Listen to my yoga, which has Maheśvara as its object."
"Behold," he said, being pleased, "I grant you divine vision. (42)
In the darkness [of ignorance], the hymn of praise to Śiva declares that there is no other whatsoever to be worshipped except you,
because of your association with the application of the word "Brahman."
O Hare, they say that the word Śiva denotes the one who performs the act of withdrawal. || 43 ||
You are superior to the universe, you are composed of the universe, O Murāri;
you are the Lord of Sacrifice, whom they praise as this very sacrifice;
you are the primordial material cause of the world, and you are its efficient cause.
O Mother, how indeed can there be non-difference between you two?
For in the praises of the Soul of the Universe, the claim of being the Lord of the Universe is consistent with that very praise of the one who holds the discus in his hand.

Furthermore, for the Lord of the universe, the conceit of being "the All" (viśvatā) is not conducive to virtue; rather, it is a cause for the degradation of one who is gripped by [attachment to] qualities. || 45 ||
Since those scriptures declare that you, O Maheśvara, preside over the universe, they figuratively attribute the nature of the universe to you;
this is understood by the wise who have mastered the secret essence of the Vedas.
But those of deluded intellect consider that very thing to be the truth. || 46 ||
O Lord, salutations to you,
the all-seeing one; for the sake of accomplishing every recitation and every application of mantras in all ritual actions, you establish that very purpose.
The sage Kātyāyana has declared thus in the Gṛhya-sūtra.
Whether it be the locus, the interval, the worship, or the worshiper—
that which exists as such is, by its very nature, a manifold manifestation of power; or rather,
the Three-Eyed One (Śiva) is to be worshipped.
The Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad states that all this is contained therein. 48.
This [hymn], taught by you, the Ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa, who are yourself the soul of sacrifice, is its expounder;
it is a hymn (sūkta) dedicated to the Puruṣa as its deity, just like the Antakāra.
They say that it is designated as having Nārāyaṇa as its seer (ṛṣi). || 49 ||
This Great Upaniṣad declares: "O Blessed One, Hiraṇyagarbha was born from you alone as the first among the gods;
yet the dull-witted call him the offspring of Nārāyaṇa."
And they prophesy there the birth of your honor from him.
"O Śiva, since you were seen by me with a glance from the lotus-like face of my forehead while my mind was absorbed in yoga, what kind of disparaging remark is this even for one such as I?"
Among these five locations, of what [nature] is there no apprehension on your part? (51)
The five Brahmans are the life-sustaining essences of your body, appearing as mantras; they are like the merit residing in the five syllables among the Rudras within the Śiva-saṃhitās of Paśupati.
The statement "in this Great Upaniṣad" is an expression of its greatness. || 52 ||
You are the Lord of Knowledge, you alone are the Lord of Beings; you are the Creator, the Sovereign who brings forth the phenomenal world—
that sovereignty of yours which was heard by the Brahmins.
Therefore, for me, that Brahmin is always the attainment of birth as Śiva. || 53 ||
O Lord of Knowledge, how could this not be stated as a mere repetition?
O Great Lord, this very sovereignty over the Vedas arises from the Veda itself;
for when the Vidyās are divided, they become hundreds.
The streams were separated like the channels of a waterless river.
That which, as the Puruṣa, presides over the disk— the treasury and repository of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman— is you;
thus [the priest] indicates you with a gesture, saying, "This is he."
By the expression "lord of beings" and by the name "moon. || 55 ||
Among these, he is called Hiraṇyapati (Lord of Gold); he is called Hiraṇyabāhu (Golden-Armed); he is called Ambikāpati (Lord of Ambikā) and Umāpati (Lord of Umā).
They call you the presiding deity of the hot-rayed sun.
O Blessed One, they are experts in the ritual of worshipping you at night.

He who knows that which blazes within the mandala, that which is its inner self, and the sovereign power belonging to these two— the Lord of Beings— as well as the fruit that one enjoys thereby; [he attains liberation].
All of this shall be explained here in due order, exactly as it is. || 57 ||
"Let all else be disregarded; those who know the mantras declare that this region was taught [by them].
The Savitṛ-verse, which is the most excellent of Savitṛ, is to be recited according to the sequence."
For they [use] the word "tarka" (reasoning) in the sense of "what indeed is your [position]? || 58 ||
This mantra is unable to name you, the Lord who presides over the sun;
for this word "bharga" takes root within you alone.
And that which you study by way of being an instructor after having taught it. || 59 ||
If this word *bharga* refers to the peaceful Enemy of Death (Śiva),
then one would have to seek another [word] that bestows fearlessness and possesses an unchanging gender, distinct from those two words which differ in their non-corresponding genders.
A position that is not heard [in scripture] is indeed illogical. || 60 ||
Whether by adding the suffix *asu* or *ghañ* to the root *śabda-smṛ*, he speaks appropriately at the end of a word in both ways with the initial vowel as udātta;
I understand this word ending in *ghañ* to have its grammatical case-role (*kāraka*) already assigned.
[He is] one whose existence as a finite entity has been refuted by the Maitrāyaṇa Śruti.
The Maitrāyaṇī Śruti, having introduced the subject with "That," and having designated Bharga as that which is to be meditated upon,
declares that Rudra is the object of the term "Bharga."
It rejects the peaceful state of the word *bharga* belonging to the Destroyer of Cities.
That peaceful state, which they call the Brāhmaṇa of the Talavakāras, does not even permit itself to be spoken;
its first quarter is determined by the sequence of question and answer.
Then his foot speaks of that very nature consisting of splendor (bharga).
Having established the indicative mark (*liṅga*) through the construction "We meditate upon Him who impels our intellect,
[He] who is *bharga*," the direct naming of the Lord, who is the primary meaning, by His own name [is expressed].
And the cessation [of the world] is also described in the words of Sāmba as "belonging to Bharga. || 64 ||
The mantra-upaniṣad itself declares you alone to be the meaning expounded by this Ṛgvedic verse:
"That syllable, that which is the most excellent of Savitṛ."
And from that, wisdom has issued forth—thus by these words. || 65 ||
This mantra, being *bhargas* as well, enters into the state of being *sāvitra* through its connection with the word *savitṛ*;
by virtue of those two respective words, it is the mantra of Maheśvara.
For those who know the mantras also recite [the names] of their respective deities. || 66 ||
We shall recite the verse dedicated to the Sun with the word "viśva" (all), the one dedicated to Śaṅkara-Viśvedevas with the word "matta" (from me),
and the ancestral rite with the word "puṣya" (prosperity).
How many indeed are such things as these? || 67 ||
Having reached the conclusion that "this is the path of the words of the Vedas," the sages remember, in the ritual of worshipping each respective deity,
the mantra of Śaṅkara with a gradual commencement.
Awaken to sound, for by it there is no worship of the Awakened One.
Even by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), having reflected upon the treasury of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman traditions, the essence was extracted;
yet even he could not perceive the pair of mantras (*mantra-dvaya*) without the inner vision.
And it was seen by Manu, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, exactly as it has been stated. || 69 ||
May he accept this entire oblation according to his desire;
may the distributor of portions take away the strength of the king from his subjects,
so that it may be offered by Pārtha to the lotus-eyed Śaṅkara.
For the night was clearly visible at your feet. || 70 ||
For your sake, O Paśupati, we have heard that the sacrificial animal is destined for slaughter;
and by that [slaughter], the product of the cow is always present in the sacrifices.
A dispute between Caṇḍeśvara and the inhabitants of heaven. || 71 ||
By virtue of their origin, they possess a connection established by Śiva; Soma, the sacrificial animal, and the oblations that exist in the cow—
all these deities receive their share in the sacrifice through his permission.
In the same way, it should be understood that [the senses] apprehend other objects as well. || 72 ||
"O Lord, there is no other bond for bound creatures than karma alone;
having obtained your permission, it must be performed by a man through your impulsion in all actions."
Those who know the mantras for the *prapada* rite take hold of the *mārambhaṇa*. || 73 ||
From the very moment of their conception, they manifested themselves to the gods headed by Prajāpati by dividing their single body;
while the oblation of Soma was being poured into the flames of the fire, they were offered as sacrifice.
O Adhvaryu, they praise your portion, O Giriśa.
All wealth is yours— whatever remains after being enjoyed by the gods, guests, dependents, and the circle of servants,
and even that which remains from the sacrifices of the Lord of Sacrifice.
He will take Maṇḍi by the hand, just as you have said. || 75 ||
In all those sacrifices which the seven groups of seven sages perform, divided according to oblations of Soma from cattle and cooked sacrificial porridges,
you are sovereign over them all without distinction.
We invoke the King for the performance of the sacrifice. || 76 ||
Let [the priest] kindle the fire accompanied by Śaṅkara and Rudra, using either the mantra "tvam agne" or the one immediately following it;
for this serves as a qualification, just as in the expression "a kingdom possessed of a king."
These two are not capable of removing the excellence of this lamp. || 77 ||
That Rohiṇī who is your deity— upon her, your two uneven glances are fixed solely upon you. Therefore,
O Lord, you are here the master of the sacrifice through these two mantras.
The wise clearly perceive [this] as having you alone as its object. (78)

Having spoken with Agni as one who has been specially distinguished by you—just as a father [speaks] to a son, a lord to a servant, or the Teacher of the Lord of Mountains (Śiva) to a disciple endowed with superior virtues—[the two of them said: Please provide the specific text you would like me to translate. You have provided the instruction, but not the source text to be translated. Once you provide the passage, I will translate it according to your requirements.
These two mantras lead one to the highest excellence. || 79 ||
The Ṛgveda Saṃhitā proclaims you as the Lord of the Earth;
this mantra declares you the King of the sacrificial rites,
the crest-jewel adorning the multitude of hymns and mantras dedicated to you.
Indeed, its power is grasped through its form as designated by its own name. || 80 ||
"O you who have been speaking for kalpas of this mantra as being yours, our protector from death, the causeless one, and supremely compassionate—
until we begin [the practice], let us consider that 'this mantra is ours'."
The root of the *Śivadharmasūkta* is known by Maheśa. || 81 ||
You are formidable; you are like the deer of Śiva, for there is no comparison for you with your splendors that rival a thousand suns risen at once.
Though your face is free from anger, by your own majesty—
From that very moment, the king became a source of fear for all embodied beings.
We meditate upon you, the uplifted thunderbolt of Giriśa; before you, the Wind, the Sun, the Fire, and Śakra tremble with fear,
as do Death and others who hold their respective offices.
These states, characterized by the nature of Brahman-hood, are the causes of fear. || 83 ||
O Blessed One, Śivā is indeed terrible, yet she is most fearsome to you; while you are being attended by her, you heal with your own terrors,
disregarding the cleansing performed by other physicians.
Through vision, he bestows even upon one whose self is Śiva.

Those who offer salutations to the Terrible One pacify [their misfortunes] through the Rudra hymns; for when afflicted, they attain relief when treated. And they satisfy Śaṅkara-Śiva with the Makānuvāka mantras.
In the case of the fire-oblation (homa), both types of mantras belong to you. || 85 ||
In the case of Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Purandara, and others,
[the *camaka* verses] are equal to the *vāja* and so forth; and in the case of other deities as well, when they are invoked, the *camaka* verses remain as the residue.
They call you, the giver and the Lord, the Wordless One.
It is not fitting for you to lead me into the presence of other gods, as a mere mortal is led before great beings;
for I am looking toward that [Lord] who grants invisibility during the performance of the sacrifice.
At the conclusion of your ritual duties, they perform the sprinkling ceremony.
Other selves are bound souls because they exist in a state of dependence; the Lord of Beasts is the Master by virtue of his sovereignty.
Those who have not attained the Upanishads speak of the Self as being without a master.
O Lord, for both [of us], the nature of both is mixed. || 88 ||
Now that you have already attained the Pāśupata doctrine of Śaṅkara, why do you choose a boon worthy of a wretched man?
You have already accepted the injunction for study for the sake of the Vedic ritual.
Whatever they recite, it is merely explanatory passages arranged like a row. || 89 ||
Moreover, because of the statements in various avadānas, your claim regarding the attainment of the Pāśupata vow must be prevented;
for how could one and the same person both receive [the initiation] and then choose [to marry]?
O Maheśvara, even many objects beyond reach can be attained.

O You who wear a garland of serpents, although Your limbs are firm, Your form is withdrawn and devoid of independent power; and those many [limbs] are internal through mantra for those who worship You.
They say that a bite from a dog is not in vain if it occurs on the tongue. || 91 ||
O Blessed One, for those men who are your devotees and whose minds are endowed with devotion, you declare that their food is never in vain;
it appears to us that this mantra is the very root within them.
Those [deeds] which were previously performed by you every day as part of the ritual of worship.
O Lord, those who praise you as having a father call you "Bharata" because of your application to acting;
for indeed, a specific designation occurs only when there is a specific cause for that designation.
There is no purpose whatsoever served by common maintenance. || 93 ||

They refute that [position] with the word "padaikadeśa" (part of a word), stating that the perception of violence is merely a part of the term "abhimāna" (pride). [This refers to the destruction of] Kāma, Antaka, Tripura, Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and so forth.
You are called a hero because of your renowned prowess. || 94 ||

In the mantra, just as the word "Agni" is seen to signify auspiciousness, so too the name "Rudra"— when occurring in proximity to words denoting violence— is not to be suspected of being [inherently] harmful.
They sow again the seed of the Rudriya-foot of the Lord of Gods. || 95 ||
O Śaṅkara, in the thousands of branches of the Vedic tradition, not only is your majesty recited through the Sāmans,
but so too, without distinction, that of you who are the sovereign lord of all souls.
The group beginning with Devavrata has been described as possessing such powers. || 96 ||
Both those princes, Skanda and Vināyaka, pointing toward their father with all their attendants,
[stood] amidst the hosts of Ṛg-verses being sung with Sāman-adjuncts from the mouths of the singers.
They cause great delight in the performance of the Śivasāman ritual, as prescribed. || 97 ||
Having set aside all else beginning with Brahmā, you have declared that for men only the one auspicious Śiva is to be meditated upon;
and having disregarded any other cause, you have stated that [Śiva alone] is the cause of liberation.
The Atharvaṇa Veda declared its completion with the word "māyā. || 98 ||
The Adhvaryu priests declare her to be your sister, O Śaṅkara, by virtue of her being the lawful wife of Dharma and established as such from birth; while they address you,
O Lord, as one approached by Atharvan.
They say that one should meditate, having abandoned the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the other [deities]. || 99 ||
O Supreme Lord, you are the one who is heard in all scriptures, the abode of truth, whom the mantras proclaim again and again;
such is the power of that Śivā, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Even the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) is unable to describe it with ease.
One face, three eyes of the Lord,
four arms, and a wondrously pure body— may that very form of yours eternally exist for the sake of benefiting the worlds.
Your divine forms become manifold. || 101 ||
Your body, having assumed the form of the Kirāta, the Lord who wields the Pināka bow, dwells together with Umā as his lawful wife; indeed,
people worship you thus on the festival day during the gathering of the gods.
